description: Hold a wet cloth at both ends and turn one hand against the other: the water runs out and the cloth winds on itself. That turning of one part of a thing against another is 'rikina', and it is what a spinner does to wool and a rope-maker to strands. 'rato' (turn) moves the whole thing round together.
articulatory_notes: A tap of the tongue tip opens into high front 'i'. The back of the tongue rises to the soft palate for 'k' and falls away into a second 'i', which carries the stress. The tip then rests on the upper teeth for 'n', and the word ends on open central 'a'.
usage_notes: A rope can twist by itself, as subject, or be twisted, as object. Strands twisted into one thing take 'muo' (INTO) for the result. In noun position 'rikina' is a twist.

examples.phi: shia muo nira ku lo sima rikina.
examples.translation: They twist the threads into cord.

semantic_domains.creation: turning fibres against each other to make thread, cord, or rope
semantic_domains.physical: one part of a thing turned against another
